Fargo at a glance

Fargo sits in the Red River Valley on the North Dakota bank of the river, with Moorhead, Minnesota directly opposite. The state line decides everything about your tax: a Fargo address means North Dakota law and a Cass County bill, while a Moorhead address means Minnesota law and another county.

Population has climbed from 90,599 in 2000 to 105,549 in 2010 and 125,990 in 2020, and the 2024 estimate is 136,285. A fire in 1893 burned 31 downtown blocks, and the brick rebuild that followed means many houses near downtown are a hundred years old or more. Buyers ask about that age, mostly in terms of wiring, plumbing and foundations.

Red River flood risk

High water is the hazard Fargo buyers think about most. Minor flooding on the Red River begins at 18 feet and major flooding at 30 feet. The river reached 39.5 feet in 1997, set a record at 40.84 feet in 2009 and hit 37 feet in 2010. The city had purchased 700 houses in flood-prone areas by 2012, and neighbors filled sandbags in 2009.

The FM Area Diversion is the permanent fix. Work began in 2017, aiming for 2027. A house in a flood-prone part of town should be disclosed as such at the start, because buyers will raise it and the offer will account for it.

Cold weather tests a Fargo house every year too. Inspectors tend to go straight to attic insulation, the furnace, basement dampness, the sump pump and the seals on windows and doors. A cash buyer folds the cost of those problems into one offer, so no list of repair demands follows an inspection.

Who values your home and who bills you

Two governments share the job. The City of Fargo assessor sets your home's value as of February 1 each year but has no control over the rate. Cass County prints the bill and collects the payment.

Each taxing body (city, county, school district, park board) adopts a budget through its elected members. Divide a body's budget need by total taxable value and you get its mill levy. Statements are mailed in early December to whoever owned the property on November 1, and your lender receives a copy if you have a mortgage.

The Cass County Finance Office at 211 9th Street South in Fargo accepts payments in person, in the mail, in the secure drop box and online. Property tax questions go to (701) 241-5600.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and penalties

Two payment styles exist. One is a single payment by February 15, which earns 5 percent off. The other is a pair of installments on March 1 and October 15. Special assessments and drain taxes ride with the first installment and never get the discount.

DateWhat happens
February 15Last day to pay in full and take the 5% discount
March 1First installment and specials due
After March 13% penalty on first installment
After May 16% total
After July 19% total
After October 1512% total on the first installment; 6% on the second

When a due date lands on a weekend or county holiday, you get the next business day, and a postmark by the deadline counts for mailed checks. Older delinquent tax also accrues 1 percent interest monthly under the county's schedule.

Section 57-20-01 of the Century Code sets the penalties, and section 57-20-09 sets the discount. Never receiving a statement does not extend the discount date.

Special assessments and drain taxes

Think of a special assessment as your share of a street, sewer or similar project built to serve your block. A drain tax is the same idea for drainage and water work. They sit on the county statement as separate lines, and the early-payment discount skips both.

You can pay a special assessment off whenever you like. Until then, one yearly installment shows up on the bill. Certain drain taxes are one-time balances, while others are recurring maintenance charges.

When you prepare to list, have the title company gather every special and drain balance still open. Buyers and lenders expect either a payoff or a plain statement of who carries the balance after the sale.

Credits and exemptions

State and city programs can shrink a Fargo bill, and each one turns on the owner's circumstances, not the buyer's. The Cass County page names the main ones:

  • Primary Residence Credit, up to $500 against 2024 taxes, filed through the State Tax Commissioner
  • Homestead Credit, for owners who are 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled
  • Disabled veteran credit, for a service-connected disability rated 50 percent or more
  • Two-year new construction abatement, which can lower taxable true and full value by $150,000

Fargo itself offers a five-year exemption for value added through remodeling of buildings 25 years old or older. Finished a renovation on an older house before listing? That added value may be outside the tax base for a while, which is worth telling the buyer.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Call the Fargo assessor first. After that, the equalization boards meet in a fixed order: local boards in the first 15 days of April, county boards in the first 10 days of June and the State Board of Equalization on the second Tuesday in August.

  • The state board can reduce a value only for owners who appealed to both local and county boards.
  • A written notice goes to each owner with the true and full value for this year and last year.
  • Still stuck after the boards? File for abatement by November 1 of the year following the payable year.

Come with proof: recent comparable sales, a professional appraisal or contractor repair quotes. Because the office values by mass appraisal, defects it cannot see from the curb are your best argument for a lower number.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing tax does not stop a sale. The balance gets paid from your proceeds at closing, and Cass County insists that the current year be paid in full before a deed can be recorded.

Behind the scenes, the title company takes the county's numbers, adds any special assessments and sends the county its payment out of your money. North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax, so what you pay at recording is a fee, not a transfer tax.

Delay adds cost. The county mails Statements of Taxes Owing in March, May, July and October, then Notices of Tax Lien in November. In May, certified Notices of Foreclosure of Tax Lien reach parcels with three years of unpaid taxes.

A practical sequence for sellers who owe:

  • Phone the Finance Office for the payoff and the date it runs through.
  • Ask the title company to list special and drain balances.
  • Compare what you will net after those payoffs under each way of selling.
  • Choose a closing date before the next penalty step.

If the debt is old, a quick sale can protect what equity you have. We will go through the county balance with you and put a written offer on the house as it stands, with no repairs and no commissions.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Fargo?

Cass County. The city's Assessment Department only sets the value, and the Finance Office at 211 9th Street South mails statements and takes payment.

When does a Fargo tax bill come due?

In halves on March 1 and October 15, or all at once by February 15 for 5 percent off. The first installment draws a penalty after March 1.

Can I sell a Fargo house that has back taxes?

Yes. The balance comes out of your closing proceeds, and the county requires the current year to be paid before it will let a deed be recorded.

Is there a deed transfer tax in North Dakota?

No deed or mortgage tax exists in the state. You will still pay normal recording fees.

What if Fargo taxes go unpaid for three years?

The parcel becomes eligible for tax lien foreclosure. Certified notices go out every May, and the owner can still pay everything up to October 1.

Bismarck, ND Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

  • Bismarck, ND Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Bismarck, ND Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Bismarck, ND Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Bismarck Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Bismarck property tax?

Who sends a Bismarck property tax bill

Two governments touch your bill. The City of Bismarck decides what the property is worth, through its Assessing Division. Burleigh County does the billing: its Auditor/Treasurer mails the statement, takes in payment and forwards the money to each taxing district monthly.

Inside Bismarck, the county's own share is under 13 percent of the total. Everything else belongs to the city, the school district and other local districts, whose levies the county cannot change. If a bill seems high, take the value question to the city assessor and the levy question to the district.

You can visit the treasurer's counter at 221 N 5th Street, Bismarck, ND 58501, and the phone is 701-222-6718. Send mail to PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506.

Bismarck at a glance

The state capital and Burleigh County seat lies on the Missouri River's east bank, facing Mandan. It had 73,622 people in the 2020 census and an estimated 77,772 in 2024. Government, hospitals and schools employ the most people, so sellers can count on a steady stream of local buyers.

With long snowy winters, buyers inspect roofs and furnaces closely. A house close to the river or a creek deserves a flood map check before you list, because the upper Missouri still floods in some seasons.

How the tax bill is calculated

The formula has four steps. The assessor sets market value, which the state calls true and full value. Half of it becomes assessed value. Taxable value is then 9 percent of assessed value on a home, or 10 percent on commercial and agricultural land. Multiply taxable value by the combined mill levy to get the tax.

The 2025 mill levy sheet shows 237.10 mills in total for the City of Bismarck taxing district. Run your own taxable value through that levy for a rough figure before credits or state-paid relief, then compare it with the statement you receive.

The same statement carries special assessments for streets, sidewalks and water and sewer lines. They stretch over several years and include principal on the borrowing, so if you have a long balance left, ask the title company how it gets paid off at closing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and penalties

The tax is due January 1, and you can pay without penalty through March 1. Pay the entire bill, specials included, by February 15 and you get a 5 percent discount. Statements go out in December, and state law requires them in the mail by December 26.

Burleigh County penalty schedule, first installment and specials
DatePenalty
March 23%
May 16%
July 19%
October 1512%

A second installment falls due October 15, and a 6 percent penalty attaches on October 16. You can pay through the county's online property search, by calling 1-800-272-9829 and giving jurisdiction code 4434, or by mailing a check to the Burleigh County Auditor. Online fees: $3.98 per e-check under $10,000 and $19.92 at $10,000 or more, or 3.61 percent on a card with a $1.52 minimum. The 5 percent discount honors a postmark on or before the deadline, though delivery by mail is not guaranteed.

How to challenge your assessment

Your first call goes to the city's Assessing Division, 701-355-1630. After that, the boards of equalization are the next stop. The city board has to meet within the first 15 days of April, the county board follows in June, and the State Board meets the second Tuesday of August. You can only reach the State Board after appearing before the other two.

The local boards hold their meetings at 221 N 5th Street. Should either one raise your value, the city has 15 days to send you written notice.

A missed board meeting is not the end: abatement is still open through the county auditor under N.D.C.C. 57-23-04. The deadline is November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent.

When property tax goes unpaid

A parcel can be foreclosed on for taxes once the tax, specials and penalties have sat unpaid into a third year. From there the county works through a set calendar:

  • Before June 1: owners and occupants receive a notice of foreclosure.
  • Before August 1: the list of delinquent parcels appears in the official county newspaper.
  • October 1: the tax lien foreclosure date, with payment in full due by 5 p.m.
  • Third Tuesday of November: the annual tax sale.

Bringing the account current ends the process at any point before the sale begins. The county gives public notice of the sale at least 15 days ahead by posting and at least 10 days ahead by publication. For a payoff that includes interest, ask the treasurer.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Credits and exemptions

The county's Tax Equalization office lists several programs. Check each against current rules before applying:

  • Homestead credit: owners who are 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, with income under $70,000 as the county lists it
  • Disabled veteran credit: honorable discharge plus a VA rating of at least 50 percent
  • Exemptions for wheelchair use, for blindness, and for a paraplegic disabled veteran
  • Farm residence exemption: requires a statement of farm gross income

Each program has its own application deadline, and a buyer may ask whether yours carries over. Call 701-222-6693 to confirm what is open before you rely on one.

Reading your Bismarck statement

Pick up the statement and sort the numbers into three groups. The first is the consolidated tax, which combines the city, school district, county and other districts under one total. The second is any special assessment, a charge for local improvements shown on a separate line. The third is the discount or penalty that applies on the date you pay.

With the county keeping only a small slice, a levy change at city hall or the school district shifts your bill far more than any decision in the treasurer's office. A seller trying to explain a jump in the bill should check the levy sheet for each taxing district first, and then ask the assessor whether the value moved.

Selling with tax due

At closing the title company takes unpaid tax and any special assessment balance out of your proceeds, so you do not need cash up front. What you do need is a payoff figure from the Burleigh County Auditor/Treasurer, with penalties through the closing date. Specials are paid through the City of Bismarck Special Assessments Department.

A cash buyer purchases the house as-is, so liens for taxes are simply part of the closing statement.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Timing a Bismarck sale around the tax year

With the bill due January 1 and the discount ending February 15, a winter listing drops the payment question into the middle of negotiations. Settle early whether the seller pays the bill before closing or the buyer's share is credited at the table. A sale in late summer or fall falls near the October 15 second installment, so the seller should confirm what has been paid and what is still open before signing a purchase agreement.

A house with years left on its special assessments raises one more question: who carries the remaining balance? Have the title company show the specials on their own line, so seller and buyer both see the figure.

Steps before you list

  1. Call the Auditor/Treasurer at 701-222-6718 and ask for a payoff covering both taxes and specials.
  2. Ask the city whether special assessments run beyond the sale date.
  3. Check the board calendar if you plan to dispute the value.
  4. Confirm any credit you hold, such as the homestead credit, and tell the title company.

With these four answers in hand, the closing statement holds few surprises. If the sale is for cash, the same payoff figures apply, though the buyer's side has no lender to satisfy, and closing can move faster once the county has confirmed the balance. The title company will want the payoff letter on paper, so ask the county to send it in writing and keep a copy with the rest of your closing documents.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property tax to in Bismarck, ND?

You pay Burleigh County. The county auditor/treasurer's office at 221 N 5th Street collects the tax, and the City of Bismarck's Assessing Division sets the value.

What is the Bismarck property tax discount?

A 5 percent discount applies to the consolidated tax if the whole bill, including specials, is paid by February 15.

When does a Bismarck tax bill become late?

The first installment is payable without penalty until March 1. A 3 percent penalty starts March 2 and rises to 12 percent on October 15. The second installment takes 6 percent after October 15.

Can I appeal my Bismarck assessment after the April meeting?

Yes, through abatement. File with the county auditor by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent, under N.D.C.C. 57-23-04.

Can I sell a Bismarck house that has unpaid taxes?

Yes. The unpaid tax and specials are paid from the proceeds at closing, so ask the county for a payoff figure before you sign.

Grand Forks at a glance

The city of Grand Forks, seat of Grand Forks County, stands beside the Red River of the North where the Red Lake River flows in. It spans about 29.3 square miles at roughly 837 feet. East Grand Forks, Minnesota, faces it across the water, and the pair make up a metro area of 104,184 people. A seller on the North Dakota bank works with Grand Forks County offices under North Dakota law. A seller across the river works under Minnesota law.

The 2020 census put the city at 59,166 people, a 12.0 percent gain over 52,838 in 2010. Median age is 30.2, typical for a university and air base town. Many local sales come after a tenant moves out or an owner takes a new job.

The 1997 flood and housing today

The 1997 Red River flood did more damage in Grand Forks than in any other major valley city that year, and a downtown fire destroyed 11 buildings at the peak. Peak flow reached about 135,000 cubic feet per second.

The city's response reshaped neighborhoods. Voluntary buyouts in 1997 and 1998 covered 850 properties. Crews demolished 694 dwellings and moved 161 houses. An English Coulee diversion channel of 9.5 miles and 12 new pump stations were built, and the project across Grand Forks and East Grand Forks cost $409 million. Levee tops are about 10 feet wide, and floodwalls add 3 feet. The city says the system could handle a 500-year flood by adding clay to the levees. Roughly 20 miles of greenway trails and a golf course now fill the old floodplain.

Buyers will ask where your lot stands in relation to the levees, so find out before you list. Winter matters too. With 48.4 inches of snow in an average year and January highs near 15.8 degrees Fahrenheit, buyers examine the roof, the furnace and the insulation closely.

Who values and who bills

City hall sets the value and the county sends the bill. The Assessing Department of the City of Grand Forks puts a value on every parcel inside city limits, appraises new construction yearly and checks claims for exemptions and credits. The County Treasurer then bills and collects.

The city walks through properties on a six-year rotation, about a sixth of them annually. An owner can refuse an interior visit, and the office then relies on what it sees outside. Find the assessing office at City Hall, 255 N 4th Street, or write to GFAssessing@grandforksgov.com.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and penalties

Bills go out by December 26. January 1 is the due date, but nothing is charged for lateness until March 1. A full-year payment by February 15 cuts the bill by 5 percent.

DateRule under N.D.C.C. 57-20-01
February 155% discount if the full year is paid
March 1First installment due; 3% penalty after
May 1Additional 3%
July 1Additional 3%
October 15Second installment due; first-installment penalty grows by 3%; second installment carries 6% after

The treasurer takes mail at PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638, and phone calls at 701-780-8292. You can also check a balance on the county's Tyler iTax and Vanguard property search pages.

Special assessments

A special assessment spreads the cost of an infrastructure project across the properties that benefit from it. The city says these are not property taxes. They can pay for sidewalks, street paving and lighting, water main, storm sewer, sanitary sewer and flood protection.

Repayment terms depend on the project type:

  • Water mains, sanitary sewer and storm sewer: 25 years
  • Paving, asphalt or concrete: 25 years
  • Street lighting, sidewalks and flood control: 20 years
  • Gravel or maintenance streets: 5 to 10 years

Questions go to the city's Finance and Administrative Services Department, 255 N 4th Street, 701-746-2671. Ask for the remaining balance before you list, because buyers and lenders will want a payoff figure.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the city. State law requires a city Board of Equalization meeting, and an appeal by letter, phone or electronic message counts as appearing in person. Written appeals can go to PO Box 5200, Grand Forks ND 58206.

  • City board: first 15 days of April
  • County board: first 10 days of June
  • State board: second Tuesday in August, and only if you appeared at the city and county boards
  • Abatement: by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes payable

Before the April meeting, collect comparable sales, an appraisal or repair bids. Evidence beats opinion at every one of these boards.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Owing tax is not an obstacle to selling. Your closing proceeds cover the county, with the title company sending the payment. Request a payoff that folds in special assessments and penalties.

The Grand Forks County Recorder, at 151 South 4th Street, phone 701-780-8262, files the deed. No deed or mortgage tax exists in North Dakota. Electronic filing is accepted through Simplifile, CSC Recording Solutions, Indecomm and ePN.

Taxes unpaid into a third year let the county foreclose its lien, and paying all that is owed by October 1 ends the threat. A Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien appears on the county website every year.

Behind already? Selling ahead of that notice leaves more choices open. Work through these in order:

  • Treasurer: tax payoff. City: special assessments.
  • Lender: mortgage payoff letter, if a loan exists.
  • Calendar: choose a closing date before the next penalty step.
  • Title company: written confirmation of every payoff.

We buy Grand Forks houses as they are, and the county payoff is handled by the title company at closing.

What the county and city each want from a seller

A Grand Forks sale touches two sets of offices, and knowing which one answers which question saves phone calls. The county Treasurer, at 701-780-8292, knows the real estate tax balance and whether anything is delinquent. The city's Finance and Administrative Services Department, at 701-746-2671, knows the special assessment balance. The Recorder, at 701-780-8262, files the deed after closing.

Ask each office for a figure dated for your closing day, not for today. Penalties step up on fixed dates, so a number that was right in March may be wrong by May. Put the three numbers together and you can see what you will net before you sign anything.

The title company usually does this legwork once a contract exists, but you can start earlier. Gather your latest statement, your mortgage payoff letter and, if you inherited the house, the estate paperwork.

How a cash sale differs

A cash buyer takes the house as it stands. You do not coordinate repairs, hold open houses or wait on a lender's approval. The county steps stay the same: taxes and specials are paid at closing, the Recorder files the deed, and the title company handles the paperwork between them.

What shortens is the calendar. A listing has to find a buyer, then clear inspection requests and loan underwriting. A cash sale skips most of that, which helps when a penalty date or a tax foreclosure date is close. Owners dealing with a tenant move, an estate or a job change often pick it for that reason. Compare the net amount from each route, counting repairs, agent fees and the months of carrying costs, before you decide.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Grand Forks?

The Grand Forks County Treasurer. The city's Assessing Department only values the property.

When is Grand Forks property tax due?

The tax is due January 1 and payable without penalty until March 1. Full payment by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount.

Can I sell a Grand Forks house with unpaid taxes?

Yes. The title company pays the taxes and any special assessments from your closing proceeds.

How large was the 1997 flood buyout?

The city bought 850 properties in its voluntary buyout in 1997 and 1998, and 694 dwellings were demolished.

Does North Dakota charge a deed tax on a sale?

No. The state has no deed or mortgage tax, although recording and title fees still apply.
